title: Frida Kahlo: what a self-portrait can contain
subtitle: A face can share its picture with a family tree, a divided landscape, an animal body or a second self.
introduction:
Kahlo's face is so familiar that it can draw attention away from the decisions surrounding it. The same direct look appears inside very different constructions: a formal dress, an exposed hospital bed, a border between countries, a thicket of animals and leaves. Sometimes the body doubles. Sometimes it changes species.

This guide follows those changes without treating every object as a code with one authorised solution. Paintings of relatives and other sitters help widen the account. So do words, frames and mirrors, which can belong to the work as materially as its painted surface. A self-portrait here is not simply a likeness accompanied by biography; it is a place where relationships can be arranged.
visitNote: This guide brings together works from several collections and private holdings. A collection name is not a current-display claim; consult the institution before travelling. Source titles and dates identify the particular versions shown. Fulang-Chang and I is represented by its painted panel, with the later mirror assembly explained in the entry.
selectionNote: Twenty editorial choices, not a complete catalogue. The selection includes explicit images of pregnancy loss, bodily injury and blood where these are part of the artwork. Reproductions retain their recorded credits and rights labels.

books.title: The Diary of Frida Kahlo: An Intimate Self-Portrait
books.author: Frida Kahlo; introduction by Carlos Fuentes; commentary by Sarah M. Lowe
books.note: The diary places painted and written pages together. Read it beside the inscriptions in the later works, while keeping its dates distinct from the earlier paintings in this guide.

books.title: Frida Kahlo: Self-Portrait with Cropped Hair
books.author: Jodi Roberts · The Museum of Modern Art, 2019
books.note: A close study of one painting from MoMA's One on One series. The linked file is a sample, not the complete book; it offers a starting point for looking more carefully at the suit, hair and written music.

works.title: Self-Portrait in a Velvet Dress
works.description: The extended neck and deep red dress create a deliberately formal self-presentation. Against it, embroidery and the restless background introduce curling movement. Kahlo's face holds a controlled position while the surrounding forms refuse to remain still. Compared with the crowded later portraits, this early painting gives proportion and fabric much of the work of defining a public appearance.

works.title: The Bus
works.description: A shared bench does not erase differences. Work clothes, a hat, a basket and a carried child distinguish passengers within the same enclosed row. The windows place them against a city without dispersing the group into it. This is a useful counterweight to the self-portraits: Kahlo also constructs pictures from the social relations among people other than herself.

works.title: Frieda and Diego Rivera
works.description: Rivera holds the palette and brushes, but Kahlo painted the picture. That distinction complicates the difference in their apparent scale. Their joined hands connect his large dark suit to her smaller, brightly dressed figure, while a written banner makes the portrait an addressed document. The image shows a partnership whose artistic work extends beyond the tools visibly assigned to one person.
works.museum: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA), San Francisco, CA, US

works.title: Henry Ford Hospital (The Flying Bed)
works.description: The hospital bed has no sheltering room. After her pregnancy loss in Detroit, Kahlo placed it before an industrial horizon and linked her body by red cords to separate anatomical and other forms. Those connections gather experiences that ordinary perspective could not contain together. The surrounding emptiness makes the patient's exposure more immediate than any attempt to decode each object separately.

works.title: Self-Portrait on the Border between Mexico and the United States
works.catalogueTitle: Self-Portrait Along the Border Line Between Mexico and the United States
works.description: Kahlo stands where the picture's two systems meet. Plants and historical forms occupy one side, factories and machinery the other; below, roots and cables provide competing networks of connection. This division is an argument about place, not a geographical survey. Her position on the pedestal lets the self-portrait hold the comparison together without making the landscapes continuous.

works.title: My Grandparents, My Parents, and I
works.catalogueTitle: My Grandparents, My Parents, and I
works.description: The red ribbon makes kinship visible. It joins generations that cannot plausibly occupy one scene at the same scale, ending with the child in the courtyard. The parents' wedding clothes give another moment in family time a place above the house. Perspective yields to genealogy: position and connection explain the relationships more clearly than a naturalistic group portrait could.

works.title: Fulang-Chang and I
works.description: The painted monkey shares Kahlo's close space among leaves and ribbon. But the familiar panel reproduction is only part of the MoMA object: a separate mirror was assembled with it after the painting was made. That addition allows a viewer's reflection to stand beside the painted company. The work's physical construction changes the terms of the portrait.

works.title: Self-Portrait Dedicated to Leon Trotsky
works.catalogueTitle: Self-Portrait Dedicated to Leon Trotsky (Between the Curtains)
works.description: Parted curtains make the standing figure appear formally presented. Flowers and an inscribed letter give her hands objects to offer, and the dedication names the portrait's recipient. Unlike the close animal portraits, this image leaves room for a public, full-length appearance. Its social purpose belongs to the composition, not merely to an anecdote added after it.
works.museum: National Museum of Women in the Arts

works.title: The Frame
works.medium: Oil on aluminium, with painted-glass surround
works.description: The flowers and birds belong to a painted-glass surround combined with the small metal portrait. They are not simply background scenery on the same surface. The overlap makes Kahlo's face appear through another object, bringing Mexican decorative craft into the construction of the work. Separating image from frame would remove a central part of its appearance.

works.title: The Two Fridas
works.description: Dress divides the seated figures; hands and a blood vessel connect them. Kahlo gives each a visible heart without making their expressions dramatically different. The doubled body carries distinctions the face alone does not display. Blood on the pale skirt makes one connection vulnerable, yet the clasped hands persist. Separation and attachment occupy the same composition.

works.title: Self-Portrait with Cropped Hair
works.description: The cut hair remains on the floor as evidence of an action. Seated in a loose suit with scissors in hand, Kahlo presents both a changed appearance and what that change has removed. Lyrics at the top introduce another voice into the image. They complicate the act's relation to love and feminine presentation without settling it into one unequivocal statement.

works.title: Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird
works.catalogueTitle: Self Portrait with Necklace of Thorns
works.description: The steady face is surrounded by things that touch, crowd or puncture its space. Thorns catch at the neck; animals appear beside the shoulders; leaves close the distance behind. That pressure is observable even without a fixed symbolic key for the hummingbird, monkey and cat. The portrait's restraint depends partly on how much activity the surrounding forms absorb.

works.title: Self-Portrait with Monkey and Parrot
works.credit: Frida Kahlo; Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires (Malba); Colección Malba. Donación Eduardo F. Costantini, 2003; WikiArt
works.description: The animals occupy opposite sides of the face but do not balance it identically. The monkey remains dark, while the green parrot approaches the colouring of the garment below. A slight turn of the head disrupts symmetry further. Repeated ingredients produce a different portrait because their colours and directions have been rearranged.
works.museum: Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires (Malba)

works.title: Self-Portrait with Monkeys
works.description: Several animal bodies leave little unoccupied space around the white blouse. Their limbs and the surrounding leaves make the figure's clear facial outline especially important. Increasing the number of companions changes the portrait's density, not just its cast. Kahlo's stillness can hold the centre because movement and overlap have been distributed around it.

works.title: Portrait of Doña Rosita Morillo
works.description: Pale yarn and knitting needles direct attention to the sitter's hands against her dark dress. Plants provide the enclosure familiar from Kahlo's self-portraits, but the older face belongs unmistakably to another person. The activity gives the hands a purpose without explaining away the sitter's expression. The repeated format leaves room for individual age and appearance.

works.title: The Broken Column
works.description: An architectural support replaces the hidden structure inside the torso, and it is fractured. Straps hold the body while nails and tears register pain at its surface. Fissures extend into the landscape behind. The painting makes bodily damage visible through an impossible construction; it need not be mistaken for a medically exact illustration to be precise about vulnerability.

works.title: The Wounded Deer
works.description: The human face preserves Kahlo's identity while the deer's body changes its capacity for movement and injury. Arrows penetrate the animal, and enclosing trunks divide the forest into narrow intervals. An opening appears beyond, but the composition supplies no clear route toward it. The hybrid figure remains caught between recognisable likeness and a body that cannot protect itself.

works.title: Diego and I
works.description: Rivera's small portrait occupies Kahlo's forehead, bringing a relationship inside the boundaries of the self-image. His additional eye makes the inset face altered rather than simply miniature. Around it, tears and loose hair concentrate attention on Kahlo's face and neck. The compression removes the need for a room or landscape to describe how the figures are connected.

works.title: Portrait of My Father
works.description: The camera identifies Guillermo Kahlo's working life, while the inscription provides an account that likeness cannot supply. Painting and writing therefore perform different kinds of remembrance. His formal clothes establish a composed appearance; the words beneath it belong to his daughter's testimony. The portrait does not ask the face alone to prove personal character.

works.title: Viva la Vida, Watermelons
works.description: The inscription, meaning “Long live life,” sits within the red flesh of a cut melon. Words remain attached to rind, seeds and uneven slices rather than floating above the still life as a slogan. With no human face in the picture, repeated colours and shapes take over the task of holding its crowded arrangement together.

closingSections.title: Keep the object beside the image
paragraphs: Compare a self-portrait with one of the portraits of other people, then return to a work that includes writing or a separate surround. The differences become clearer when familiar biography does not do all the explaining. Consult the holding institution for current display, and check reproduction rights independently; a freely circulating image is not a licence.
